descriptions.description:
Second versioned deposit accompanying the v22 P6-ERIS manuscript submitted to Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability (IOP Publishing). This is a New Version on concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21827667. The v1.0.0 deposit (6 August 2026) accompanied the ERIS-100994 submission that was returned without external review on scientific-reporting-standards and reference-comprehensiveness vectors. The v2.0.0 deposit delivers a substantially strengthened manuscript following a demanding push cycle: 6 audit rounds + publishability rewrite + real empirical execution on the SSI Index v4.23 canonical + language strengthening + academic register sweep + three-country cross-country identification.

The paper delivers three contributions on a per-substation-catchment classifier of grid maladaptation mode across the OECD grid.

Contribution 1 (Framework). The three-mode classifier {Renewal-pipeline, Siting, Topology} operates as a decision layer over the shared SSI Index v4.23 ridge estimator via softmax weight-vector projection with hard-constraint eligibility filter e(i) and bootstrap-stability score s(i). Four-path cross-consistency envelope — Path A composition-averaged Byers-parity baseline, Path B Gaussian-copula rank-transform, Path C ridge headline (α_opt = 92.4, R² = 0.851 at Italian pilot depth), Path C̃ ERA5-Land direct predictor design (α_opt = 0.001, R² = 0.180, ‖β̂_ERA5‖₂ = 0.104 at n = 47,906) — anchors the identified envelope. Statistical rigor stack: Kish two-tier country-in-region clustering K_eff ≈ 6, Cameron-Gelbach-Miller cluster-robust SE, Benjamini-Yekutieli FDR positive-dependence variant at q ≤ 0.05, SALib Saltelli-Sobol variance decomposition, Gelman-Hill partial-pooling Bayesian via PyMC v5 with Half-Cauchy(0, 2.5) prior under NUTS, 10,000-replication Gaussian bootstrap, MacKinnon-Webb wild-cluster bootstrap-t, 5,000-permutation independence check, Arkhangelsky synthetic-DiD placebo. Sobol variance decomposition on classifier p(Siting) versus R_median composite demonstrates empirically-measurable net-new information beyond the shared ridge: R8_adapt +0.580, R10 +0.120, R6d +0.129 (differential total-order sensitivity index) against R6c_flood dominance in scalar R_median (S_T = 0.722).

Contribution 2 (Cross-country identification within-country cross-validation across three-country pilot). At Italian pilot depth of 47,906 catchments across 20 Regioni, held-out cross-validation (Train Northern + Central 30,974 → Test Southern + Islands 16,558) delivers 99.29% classification accuracy. UK pilot at 62,409 catchments across 12 ITL-1 regions with Ofgem RIIO regulatory anchor: held-out cross-validation (Train Southern 32,144 → Test Northern + Celtic 26,155) delivers 91.93%. Japan pilot at 7,073 catchments across 8 macro-regions with METI + OCCTO regulator anchors (Tier-2 register-access): held-out cross-validation (Train Honshu → Test Peripheral) delivers 97.84%. Three-country consistency verdict is strong: R8_adapt top-1 Sobol S_T concordant across all three countries (Italy 0.624, UK 0.602, Japan 0.527); Spearman rank correlation on seven shared modifiers is positive across all pairs (Italy-UK 0.643, Italy-Japan 0.750, UK-Japan 0.821). Country-specific risk architecture surfaces through rank-2 modifier variation: Italy R10-just, UK R10-just, Japan R6-seismic (rank 2, S_T = 0.259) — empirical evidence the classifier detects country-specific risk architecture without losing cross-country consistency on the identifying R8_adapt anchor. BY-FDR against per-country cohort mean surfaces substantive-magnitude outliers: Italy Calabria (RP +12.2 pp) + Basilicata (Topology +6.6 pp); UK Wales (RP +10.4 pp) + Scotland (Siting +11.3 pp) + Northern Ireland (RP +8.5 pp); Japan Kanto (TEPCO metropolitan compound signature) + Kyushu (Siting +10.3 pp) + Chugoku (Siting +9.4 pp). The May 2023 Emilia-Romagna flood serves as illustrative case study of the classifier-cascade nexus; the cascade-coefficient identification anchor is attributed to companion Bérard 2026 (Environmental Research: Energy, under review) at synthetic-DiD placebo p = 0.012.

Contribution 3 (Register-access-readiness audit protocol). A 4-tier generalisable procedural framework classifies 40 OECD countries plus Greenland via three coded data classes (RAB depreciation register, TYNDP siting outcomes, TYNDP topology graphs) into Tier 1 (n = 25, ENTSO-E members plus Norway plus Switzerland plus Australia), Tier 2 (n = 7, Chile, Greece, Israel, Japan, Korea, New Zealand, US), Tier 3 (n = 7, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Turkey). Three NUTS-3-proxy placebo p-values (Sardegna 2023, Calabria 2024, Iberian April 2025) illustrate the protocol's diagnostic value at Tier-3 register-access scale (all three p-values indistinguishable from null).

The snapshot represents the full discipline arc from ERIS-100994 desk-reject through 22 manuscript versions: diagnostic memo, three-contribution architecture design, four-pass rewrite (v13), six audit rounds (v14-v17), publishability rewrite (v18), real Italian Phase 1 execution on SSI Index v4.23 canonical (v19), empirical corrections (Path C̃ ERA5 landed, BY-FDR substantive-baseline reframe, regional-heterogeneity narrative empirically corrected — v20), UK second-country anchor (v21), academic register sweep (v21 to v22), Japan third-country anchor (v22), Pascal compression to ERIS ceiling. Frozen against SSI Index v4.23 canonical (15 July 2026 TERMINAL snapshot).

Underlying per-substation payload builds on GHSL 5 km catchment population, Niva 2023 20-year sum migration score, polygon spatial-join socio-economic backfill across 25 countries via Eurostat GISCO NUTS-3 2024 and GADM 4.1 admin1, per-country min-max semantic normalisation of migration_score into [0, 1] envelope preserving per-substation ranking, and per-substation ERA5-Land climate trajectory {I₁, I₂, I₃} resident in the canonical.

Reproducibility ladder: Layer 1 pipeline scripts at deterministic κ = 1.0 (this Zenodo deposit); Layer 2 SHA-256-locked results-JSON manifest (SHA256SUMS.txt inside archive); Layer 3 institutional registers (ARERA + Terna for Italy, Ofgem + National Grid ET for UK, METI + OCCTO for Japan, ENTSO-E + JRC EFAS + Copernicus EMS + INGV + EFFIS + CMIP6 ISIMIP3 for cohort-wide anchors). CC BY 4.0 (data + manuscript) + MIT (code); Docker + Python 3.10.9.

Visibly-honest degradation preserved throughout: (1) Val d'Aosta n=58 fleet-insufficient marker; (2) Convention #56 residual buckets for unmapped county-to-ITL-1 (UK 4,110 subs = 6.6%) and unmapped prefecture-to-macro-region (Japan 16 subs = 0.23%) surfaced honestly; (3) full-cohort HDI on cross-country Bayesian pooling crosses zero (μ_cohort = -0.682, HDI95 [-1.707, +0.310]) — reduced-cohort excluding four †-flagged R7_cyber-drift outliers (Canada, Finland, Mexico, Turkey) at μ_reduced = +0.421 also with envelope crossing zero; consistency with Contribution 3's register-access-readiness taxonomy interpretation; (4) Emilia-Romagna DiD cascade-coefficient identification honestly attributed to companion paper

titles.title: Curvas de fragilidad de inundación por tsunami en Coquimbo por Aránguiz et al. (2018)

descriptions.description: El terremoto de septiembre de 2015 en Coquimbo, con magnitud $M_W = 8.3$, tuvo como consecuencia un daño localizado en áreas bajas de la ciudad. Considerando esta situación, los autores del artículo Development and application of a tsunami fragility curve of the 2015 tsunami in Coquimbo, Chile desarrollaron tres curvas de fragilidad para la ciudad de Coquimbo basadas en datos obtenidos en terreno con respecto a los daños y simulaciones numéricas de tsunamis. Las curvas de fragilidad desarrolladas estiman la probabilidad de daño de la ciudad en base al número de edificios dañados con respecto a tres variables de los tsunamis: **profundidad de inundación**, **velocidad** y la **fuerza hidrodinámica**. Las curvas fueron ajustadas utilizando una distribución normal, es decir $\displaystyle F\left(\text{IM}, \mu, \sigma\right) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ 1 + \text{erf}\left( \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma \sqrt{2}} \right) \right]$ donde - $\text{IM}$ es la medida de intensidad: profundidad de inundación (m), velocidad (ms$^{\text{-1}}$) o fuerza hidrodinámica (kNm$^{\text{-1}}$) - $\mu$ es la media de la medida de intensidad escogida - $\lambda$ es la desviación estándar de la medida de intensidad escogida - $\text{erf}$ es la función de error de Gauss Además se indica el valor de $R^2$ correspondiente al coeficiente de determinación entre los datos y el modelo propuesto.

titles.title: Water User Profiles — Surveys in the Longaví River Basin (Chile)

dates.dateInformation: Survey in Longaví River sub-Basin, Maule Region, Chile, Study area  -36.0 ; -71.5

descriptions.description:
This database contains the results of 268 face-to-face surveys administered to water users in the Longaví River basin, Maule Region, Chile. The instrument was designed to characterise the socioeconomic, productive, and organisational profile of water rights holders and users, as well as their perceptions regarding water management, extreme climate events (droughts and floods), and climate change.

The questionnaire comprises 104 variables (questions) organised into the following thematic modules:

1. Farm identification and property data (irrigation canal, land tenure    status, municipality).2. Sociodemographic profile (age, gender, educational level).3. Water rights ownership and participation in Water User Organisations (WUOs).4. Water source, irrigation technology, water turn system, and abstraction method.5. Agricultural production, marketing, and productive challenges.6. Knowledge of the Water Code and basin-level participation.7. Flood recovery and institutional support received.8. Attitudes towards collective action and the Junta de Vigilancia.9. Conflicts among water users.10. Technical and financial assistance.11. Perceptions of climate change and future scenarios.

The data were collected as part of an organisational strengthening process of the Junta de Vigilancia del Río Longaví (JVRL).

The dataset has been anonymised: variables that allowed individual identification of respondents have been removed (surveyor name, respondent's first name, and phone number). Each record is identified by an anonymous code (id_respondente: R001 to R268).

Files are provided in CSV (UTF-8 with BOM, comma-separated), XLSX, and ODS formats. A variable dictionary (codebook) is also included, containing the original question text and the possible values for each column.

titles.title: Replication Data for: After the Flood: Disasters, Ideological Voting and Electoral Choices in Chile

descriptions.description: Can natural disasters affect voters’ electoral choices, and in particular, ideological voting? Even as climate change has increased concerns about the frequency and intensity of disasters, the effects of these negative events on voter behavior are not yet fully understood. Though ideological labels are known to be informative heuristics, the literature has thus far overlooked their role after natural hazards. Might affected citizens become more likely to select candidates with an ideology that can be associated with what victims need after a disaster? Answering this question is difficult since disaster damage can be correlated with multiple victims’ unobserved characteristics. To address this challenge, I use a natural experiment created by the floods that occurred in Chile in 2015 to take advantage of random variation in citizens’ exposure to a disaster. I then capture voters’ electoral choices using a conjoint survey experiment. The findings show that material damage caused by this disaster increased the probability of voters selecting left-wing and independent candidates. Qualitative evidence from interviews helps to illuminate the causal mechanisms underlying these results.

Activation date: 2018-07-27
Event type: Flood

Activation reason:
The activation focuses on two flood disaster management levels.The first refers to post‐disaster situation analysis concerning the impact of intense rain (16 December 2017) over the Villa Santa Lucia, in the commune of Chaitén, Chile (CL).Mudflow Delineation - Damage AssessmentComprehensive knowledge of the disaster is provided through a number of information layers, as is the spatial extent of the flood/ landslide (mudslide) caused by the rainfall, the impact on population and assets, as well as information on Land Use/Cover and existing assets and infrastructures.      The second refers to the efficient support of flood risk management activities and planning of prevention, protection and preparedness measures through accounting for the areas characteristics.Flood Risk Mapping - Population at RiskTowards reducing the adverse consequences of flooding for both population and economic activity (pre-disaster) flood risk assessment was implemented within a large area: the valleys connecting Futaleufú, Palena, Villa Vanguardia, Villa Santa Lucia and Puerto Cárdenas. The Hazard layer is based on the Flood Susceptibility Index, calculated from the DEM according to Samela, C., Troy, T. J., & Manfreda, S. (2017). Geomorphic classifiers for flood-prone area delineation for data-scarce environments. Advances in Water Resources, 102, 13-28.Exposure is defined on the basis of Asset Category in the areas located inside a flood hazard area. To each category a specific level of vulnerability is assigned.The vulnerability assessment of the exposed elements was calculated by considering specific criteria that characterize flood vulnerability and distinguish urban from non-urban areas.The risk level is mapped combining hazard and vulnerability through specific lookup tables.Mitigation measures are defined in terms of level of risk for bridges, urban structural and non-structural measures and river structural measures.Flood Risk Mapping - Assets and Transportation Network at Risk

titles.title: A Modified Atmospheric River Scale for Flood Hazards

attributes.publisher: Consortium of Universities for the Advancement of Hydrologic Science, Inc

rightsList.rights: This resource is shared under the Creative Commons Attribution CC BY.

descriptions.description:
Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are key drivers of regional water supply and flood hazard in subtropical and mid-latitude regions, generating interwoven beneficial and hazardous impacts. The original AR scale, developed for early-warning communication, ranks ARs from 1 (“primarily beneficial”) to 5 (“primarily hazardous”) based on atmospheric vapor transport. However, the AR scale does not account for physical processes on the land surface that can strongly influence flood response. Analyzing over 70,000 AR landfalls across 142 catchments in California and central Chile, here we show that runoff efficiency, primarily controlled by antecedent soil moisture, is the dominant source of peak streamflow variability not explained by the AR scale. Based on this insight, we present a simple modification to the AR scale for flood hazards that incorporates antecedent moisture conditions. This modification close to doubles the scale’s correspondence with peak streamflow and increases the number of flood-generating ARs classified as hazardous by over 30%, raising AR flood detection rates to 81% in California and 64% in central Chile. These findings demonstrate that incorporating critical land surface conditions into hazard classification can enhance early-warning tools for communicating hazard likelihood.

See Webb, M. J. et al. Antecedent moisture enhances early warning of atmospheric river flood hazards. Nat Commun https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69286-3 (2026) doi:10.1038/s41467-026-69286-3.

titles.title: Implementation of four conceptual rainfall-runoff models to simulate drought-to-flood transitions in Chile and Switzerland

descriptions.description:
Here, we present the calibrated parameters for the different 60 KGE configurations (5 KGE formulations x 3 streamflow transformations x 4 weights), 4 hydrological models (GR4J, GR5J, GR6J, and TUW), and 63 catchments (24 in Chile and 39 in Switzerland; see "_Study_domain_filter_v2025_v4.png") used to prepare the manuscript “How well do hydrological models simulate streamflow extremes and drought-to-flood transitions” submitted for consideration for publication in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences (HESS). Additionally, performance metrics and figures for the observed and simulated transitions are included.

Each ZIP file contains several CSV data files and PNG images (see "Folders_structure.png"). The name of the folders is given by the database (i.e., CAMELS-CL or CAMELS-CH), followed by the code associated with the station (id_gauge). Thus, the file "camelscl_5722002.zip" corresponds to the catchment with code 5722002 associated with the CAMELS-CL database.

Additionally, two zip folders are included, containing:



Basic_Scripts.zip: Basic R-functions used to configure the hydrological models, identify streamflow extreme events and their transitions, and analyze the ability of models to capture such events.

summary.zip: Compilation of the results retrieved from the analysis of the simulations across catchments (i.e. merge the '02_Analysis_DDS' folders).

titles.title: MAAT, MAP and pH in soils and peats

descriptions.description: Branched glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraethers (brGDGTs) are a family of bacterial lipids which have emerged over time as robust temperature and pH paleoproxies in continental settings. Despite improvements in brGDGT analytical methods and development of refined models, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) associated with global calibrations between brGDGT distribution and MAAT in soils and peats remains high (~ 5 °C). Here we proposed to extend the global brGDGT terrestrial dataset previously proposed (n = 663; Dearing Crampton-Flood et al., 2019) with 112 soil samples from 6 altitudinal transects located in France (n = 49), Italy (n = 24), Tibet (n = 17), Chile (n = 8) and Peru (n =14). The transects were selected to take into account as much climatic and environmental variability as possible. All of these surficial soil samples (0 -10 cm depth) cover a wide range of temperatures (0°C to 26°C) and pH (3 to 8) and are representative of a wide diversity of environmental variables, vegetation and soil type. These new data were combined with previously published ones. This allowed the development of a new global terrestrial brGDGT temperature calibration from a worldwide extended dataset (i.e. 775 soil and peat samples) using a machine learning algorithm. This new model, called random Forest Regression for PaleOMAAT using brGDGTs (FROG), represents a refined brGDGT temperature calibration (R² = 0.8; RMSE = 4.01°C) for soils and peats, more robust and accurate than previous global soil calibrations while being proposed on an extended dataset.

Thus, the file "camelscl_5722002.zip" corresponds to the catchment with code 5722002 associated with the CAMELS-CL database. The files inside each folder are described below:



_Figures_conDF/ : visualizations of observed drought-to-flood transitions (rapid and seasonal) compared to model simulations.

conDF_events_database_id-gauge.csv: Contains event-based data for the catchment.

Summary_conDF_delta_avg_database_id-gauge.csv: Summary of delta average values across different events.

Summary_conDF_delta_perc_avg_database_id-gauge.csv: Summary of percentage delta averages.

Summary_conDF_events_database_id-gauge.csv: Summarized dataset of hydrological events.

Summary_conDF_obs_avg_database_id-gauge.csv: Observed data averages.

Summary_Detection_database_id-gauge.csv: Detection metrics related to drought-to-flood transitions.

Summary_KGE_database_id-gauge.csv: Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) values for model performance assessment.

Summary_KGE_eval_database_id-gauge.csv: (Cross-) Evaluation of KGE for the different configurations tested.

Summary_GOF_variable_database_id-gauge.csv: Goodness-of-Fit (GOF) values for model performance assessment. The variables analyzed were streamflow (Q), snow water equivalent (SWE), actual evapotranspiration (ET), and surface soil moisture (SM).

Summary_Sign_variable_database_id-gauge.csv: Hydrological signatures values for model performance assessment. The variables analyzed were streamflow (Q), snow water equivalent (SWE), actual evapotranspiration (ET), and surface soil moisture (SM).

_Summary_params_model_database_id-gauge.csv: Calibrated parameter set for the hydrological model according to the 60 different configurations tested. The models analyzed were GR4J, GR5J, GR6J, and TUW.


Additionally, two zip folders are included, containing:



Basic_Scripts.zip: Basic R-functions used to configure the hydrological models, identify streamflow extreme events and their transitions, and analyze the ability of models to capture such events.

statistical_analysis.zip: Results associated with the Wilcoxon test at a 5% significance level applied to assess the statistical significance of the differences between the configurations tested in this study. The differences are analyzed in absolute terms, keeping different choices fixed to assess differences due to one of them (e.g., changes due to the applications of weights), and in relative terms with respect to the unweighted HiLo original KGE formulation (i.e., reference).


### Note on dataset versions:v1.0: [19.02.2025] Original version with results per catchment.v1.5: [11.09.2025] Same as v1.0, but now including one folder with some R-scripts useful for model configuration and streamflow extreme event detection, and another one with results associated with statistical significance tests.

descriptions.description:
This starter data kit collects extracts from global, open datasets relating to climate hazards and infrastructure
  systems.




  These extracts are derived from global datasets which have been clipped to the national scale (or subnational, in
  cases where national boundaries have been split, generally to separate outlying islands or non-contiguous regions),
  using Natural Earth (2023) boundaries, and is not meant to express an opinion about borders, territory or sovereignty.




  Human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of climate and weather extremes. This is causing
  widespread, adverse impacts to societies, economies and infrastructures. Climate risk analysis is essential to inform
  policy decisions aimed at reducing risk. Yet, access to data is often a barrier, particularly in low and middle-income
  countries. Data are often scattered, hard to find, in formats that are difficult to use or requiring considerable
  technical expertise. Nevertheless, there are global, open datasets which provide some information about climate
  hazards, society, infrastructure and the economy. This "data starter kit" aims to kickstart the process and act as a
  starting point for further model development and scenario analysis.



Hazards:


  
coastal and river flooding (Ward et al, 2020; Baugh et al, 2024)
  
extreme heat and drought (Russell et al 2023, derived from Lange et al, 2020)
  
tropical cyclone wind speeds (Russell 2022, derived from Bloemendaal et al 2020 and Bloemendaal et al 2022)



Exposure:


  
population (Schiavina et al, 2023)
  
built-up area (Pesaresi et al, 2023)
  
roads (OpenStreetMap, 2025)
  
railways (OpenStreetMap, 2025)
  
power plants (Global Energy Observatory et al, 2018)
  
power transmission lines (Arderne et al, 2020)



Contextual information:


  
elevation (European Union and ESA, 2021)
  
land-use and land cover (Copernicus Climate Change Service and Climate Data Store, 2019)
  
administrative boundaries from geoBoundaries (Runfola et al., 2020)




  The spatial intersection of hazard and exposure datasets is a first step to analyse vulnerability and risk to
  infrastructure and people.




  To learn more about related concepts, there is a free short course available through the Open University on
  Infrastructure and Climate Resilience.
  This overview of the course has more details.




  These Python libraries may be a useful place to start analysis of the data in the packages produced by this workflow:




  

    snkit helps clean network data
  
  

    nismod-snail is designed to help implement infrastructure
    exposure, damage and risk calculations

  repository contains a larger workflow for global-scale open-data infrastructure risk and resilience analysis.

  and future flooding risks to transport networks in East Africa, which has a related online visualisation tool at
  https://east-africa.infrastructureresilience.org/

titles.title: Implementation of four conceptual rainfall-runoff models to simulate drought-to-flood transitions in Chile and Switzerland

descriptions.description:
Here, we present the calibrated parameters for the different 60 KGE configurations (5 KGE formulations x 3 streamflow transformations x 4 weights), 4 hydrological models (GR4J, GR5J, GR6J, and TUW), and 63 catchments (24 in Chile and 39 in Switzerland; see "_Study_Domain_filter_v2025.png") used to prepare the manuscript “How well do hydrological models simulate streamflow extremes and drought-to-flood transitions” submitted for consideration for publication in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences (HESS). Additionally, performance metrics and figures for the observed and simulated transitions are included.

Each ZIP file contains several CSV data files and PNG images organized within a folder named in the same way as the ZIP file.  The name of the folders is given by the database (i.e., CAMELS-CL or CAMELS-CH), followed by the code associated with the station (id_gauge). Thus, the file "camelscl_5722002.zip" corresponds to the catchment with code 5722002 associated with the CAMELS-CL database. The files inside each folder are described below:



_Figures_conDF/ : visualizations of observed drought-to-flood transitions (rapid and seasonal) compared to model simulations.

conDF_events_database_id-gauge.csv: Contains event-based data for the catchment.

Summary_conDF_delta_avg_database_id-gauge.csv: Summary of delta average values across different events.

Summary_conDF_delta_perc_avg_database_id-gauge.csv: Summary of percentage delta averages.

Summary_conDF_events_database_id-gauge.csv: Summarized dataset of hydrological events.

Summary_conDF_obs_avg_database_id-gauge.csv: Observed data averages.

Summary_Detection_database_id-gauge.csv: Detection metrics related to drought-to-flood transitions.

Summary_KGE_database_id-gauge.csv: Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) values for model performance assessment.

Summary_KGE_eval_database_id-gauge.csv: (Cross-) Evaluation of KGE for the different configurations tested.

Summary_GOF_variable_database_id-gauge.csv: Goodness-of-Fit (GOF) values for model performance assessment. The variables analyzed were streamflow (Q), snow water equivalent (SWE), actual evapotranspiration (ET), and surface soil moisture (SM).

Summary_Sign_variable_database_id-gauge.csv: Hydrological signatures values for model performance assessment. The variables analyzed were streamflow (Q), snow water equivalent (SWE), actual evapotranspiration (ET), and surface soil moisture (SM).

_Summary_params_model_database_id-gauge.csv: Calibrated parameter set for the hydrological model according to the 60 different configurations tested. The models analyzed were GR4J, GR5J, GR6J, and TUW.

descriptions.description: Branched glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraethers (brGDGTs) are a family of bacterial lipids which have emerged over time as robust temperature and pH paleoproxies in continental settings. Despite improvements in brGDGT analytical methods and development of refined models, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) associated with global calibrations between brGDGT distribution and MAAT in soils and peats remains high (~ 5 °C). Here we proposed to extend the global brGDGT terrestrial dataset previously proposed (n = 663; Dearing Crampton-Flood et al., 2019) with 112 soil samples from 6 altitudinal transects located in France (n = 49), Italy (n = 24), Tibet (n = 17), Chile (n = 8) and Peru (n =14). The transects were selected to take into account as much climatic and environmental variability as possible. All of these surficial soil samples (0 -10 cm depth) cover a wide range of temperatures (0°C to 26°C) and pH (3 to 8) and are representative of a wide diversity of environmental variables, vegetation and soil type. These new data were combined with previously published ones. This allowed the development of a new global terrestrial brGDGT temperature calibration from a worldwide extended dataset (i.e. 775 soil and peat samples) using a machine learning algorithm. This new model, called random Forest Regression for PaleOMAAT using brGDGTs (FROG), represents a refined brGDGT temperature calibration (R² = 0.8; RMSE = 4.01°C) for soils and peats, more robust and accurate than previous global soil calibrations while being proposed on an extended dataset.

descriptions.description: This dataset reports 87Sr/86Sr and 144Nd/143Nd results of a series of sediment samples collected in Chilean Patagonia (47.0–48.5°S), including (1) suspended sediments from the mouth of seven rivers, (2) eight grain-size fractions of a bulk river sediment sample, and (3) seven subsamples taken from a fjord sediment core. All results were obtained on a MC-ICP-MS at the University of Missouri Research Reactor.

titles.title: At-site flood frequency analysis results for 88 catchments in continental Chile

descriptions.description: This dataset contains climate and physiographic descriptors for 88 near-natural catchments located in Chile, between the Atacama and Araucania regions. Further, at-site flood frequency analysis results are reported for several return periods, along with maximum catchment-scale daily precipitation.
